causal_assumptions.consistency: Each signal condition follows the reported response-contingent test procedure.
causal_assumptions.exchangeability: Stimulus orientation and signal assignments were counterbalanced within participants.
causal_assumptions.interference: Online participants were assumed not to influence one another's responses.
causal_assumptions.positivity: Each included participant experienced both trained-signal and control test contingencies.

claims.causal_estimand: Within-participant difference in test avoidance responding when a response produces the trained safety signal versus the experiment-specific control consequence.

confidence.rationale: Three full-test contrasts supported the effect, one similar-signal comparison was null, and Experiment 5's full-session main effect was marginal although total signal choices and the first four trials differed.

limitations: Experiments 1-4 did not isolate conditioned reinforcement from every possible sensory or generalization account.
Experiments 1-3 were repeated after unpreregistered exclusion decisions; Experiment 5 was preregistered.

boundary_conditions: Generalization depends on perceptual similarity between trained and control signals.
Participants who never produced a safety signal during training were excluded from reported analyses.
scope.population: Healthy adults completing Fisher and Urcelay's online or laboratory avoidance tasks.
scope.temporal_scope: Immediate extinction test after instrumental avoidance training.

claims.statement: In Fisher and Urcelay's human extinction tests, making a trained safety signal contingent on responding increased avoidance relative to no signal or a dissimilar signal in several experiments; the effect was absent with a similar-signal control and was analysis-sensitive in the new-response test.
claims.temporal_ordering: Signal contingency is assigned to ambiguous stimuli before test responding is measured.

confidence.rationale: Controlled behavioral contrasts support reinforcing function, but perceptual generalization and sensory reinforcement delimit the interpretation.

claims.falsifiable_boundary: The account is challenged when adequately powered, preregistered tests with perceptually matched controls repeatedly show no contingency-specific increase in responding.

boundary_conditions: Does not identify subjective relief as the mediator.
Does not imply that every safety signal reinforces every avoidance response.
scope.population: Healthy human participants in response-produced safety-signal tasks.
scope.temporal_scope: Instrumental training followed by immediate extinction testing.

claims.statement: A learned safety signal produced by an avoidance response can function as a conditioned reinforcer and thereby increase later avoidance responding.
claims.temporal_ordering: Safety-signal training precedes the response-contingent test and measured response differences.

causal_assumptions.consistency: Fractal choices produced outcomes according to programmed task probabilities.
causal_assumptions.exchangeability: Fractal-to-condition assignment was counterbalanced across participants.
causal_assumptions.positivity: Participants repeatedly encountered both action alternatives.

claims.causal_estimand: Difference in selection probability for actions assigned lower versus higher monetary-loss probability.

confidence.rationale: Counterbalanced programmed contingencies support a narrow causal interpretation, but the sample was small and the test was one-tailed.

limitations: Does not establish subjective relief or a specific neural signal as the mediator.

boundary_conditions: Restricted to probabilistic monetary loss and the tested fractal choices.
scope.population: Sixteen healthy right-handed adults in the specified monetary instrumental task.
scope.temporal_scope: Two sessions of repeated instrumental choices.

claims.statement: In Kim et al.'s monetary task, assigning one action a lower probability of loss increased preference for that action over repeated trials.
claims.temporal_ordering: Counterbalanced outcome probabilities governed feedback before preference was estimated.

causal_assumptions.consistency: Active and yoked assignments corresponded to the reported grid-control and motor-control procedures.
causal_assumptions.exchangeability: Supported by random group assignment and paired yoked outcome exposure.
causal_assumptions.interference: Each yoked pair shared an outcome schedule by design but pairs were otherwise independent.
causal_assumptions.positivity: Participants were assigned to both active and yoked conditions.

claims.causal_estimand: Between-group effect of active instrumental shock control versus yoked extinction on next-day conditioned skin-conductance responding.

confidence.rationale: Random assignment and yoked shock exposure isolate instrumental control, but the extraction is based on one study and no standardized effect was recorded here.

limitations: Yoked pairing is deliberate partial interference and is included in the estimand.
Neural differences do not by themselves identify the behavioral mediator.

boundary_conditions: Outcome is conditioned physiological responding, not future avoidance frequency.
scope.population: Fifty-six analyzed healthy adults randomly assigned to active-control or yoked-extinction groups.
scope.temporal_scope: Active-control training on day 1 and cue-only retrieval 23-25 hours later.

claims.statement: Random assignment to active shock control, compared with yoked extinction, altered conditioned skin-conductance responding on the following day.
claims.temporal_ordering: Group assignment and day-1 learning preceded the day-2 cue-only retrieval test.

evidence.design: Online within-participant extinction test; trained safety signal versus no-signal consequence, counterbalanced across novel Gabor stimuli.

effect.metric: partial eta squared for main effect of trained signal versus no signal
effect.notes: F(1,71)=16.28, p<0.001 across eight test trials.

evidence.extraction_locator: Results, Experiment 1; Materials and Methods, Participants and Test.
limitations: No-signal comparison cannot fully exclude generic sensory reinforcement.
Reported sample excludes participants who earned no training safety signal; replication decision was not preregistered.
evidence.population: Healthy adults recruited online; reported analysis after training-experience criterion.
evidence.summary: Participants emitted more avoidance responses when responding produced the trained safety signal than when it produced no signal.

evidence.design: Online within-participant extinction test; trained safety signal versus a new signal differing only in color.

effect.metric: F statistic for main effect of trained versus similar new signal
effect.notes: F(1,54)=0.003, p=0.958; total signal counts also did not differ, t(54)=1.018, p=0.31.

evidence.extraction_locator: Results, Experiment 2; Materials and Methods, Participants and Test.
limitations: Null contrast does not distinguish true equivalence from generalization between perceptually similar signals.
evidence.population: Healthy adults recruited online; reported analysis after training-experience criterion.
evidence.summary: Avoidance did not differ when trained and control signals differed only in color, consistent with broad signal generalization or no specific reinforcement effect.

evidence.design: Online within-participant extinction test; trained safety signal versus a new signal differing in color and shape.

effect.metric: partial eta squared for main effect of trained versus dissimilar new signal

evidence.extraction_locator: Results, Experiment 3; Materials and Methods, Participants and Test.
limitations: Dissimilar control reduces but does not eliminate every sensory-reinforcement account.
evidence.population: Healthy adults recruited online; reported analysis after training-experience criterion.
evidence.summary: Participants responded more for the trained safety signal than for a perceptually dissimilar new signal.

evidence.design: Laboratory within-participant extinction test using a 95 dB tone; trained safety signal versus no signal.

effect.metric: partial eta squared for main effect of trained signal versus no signal
effect.notes: F(1,40)=6.20, p=0.017 across eight test trials.

evidence.extraction_locator: Results, Experiment 4; Materials and Methods, Participants and Test.
limitations: No-signal comparison remains susceptible to generic sensory reinforcement.
Final analyzed sample was 41 after the training-experience criterion.
evidence.population: Healthy university participants; reported analysis after training-experience criterion.
evidence.summary: The laboratory experiment replicated greater responding for a trained safety signal using a loud-tone aversive outcome.

evidence.design: Preregistered online choice test transferring from space-bar avoidance to mouse-click choice; trained versus dissimilar new signal.

effect.metric: Cohen d for total trained-signal versus new-signal choices
effect.notes: Total signal counts differed, t(53)=2.89, p=0.006. The preregistered full eight-trial ANOVA signal effect was marginal, F(1,53)=3.29, p=0.075; a first-four-trial analysis was significant, p=0.023.

evidence.extraction_locator: Results, Experiment 5; Materials and Methods, Participants and Test.
limitations: Interpretation depends on outcome metric and analysis window.
Reported sample excludes participants who produced no training safety signal.
evidence.population: Healthy adults recruited online; reported analysis after training-experience criterion.
evidence.summary: Choice totals favored the trained safety signal, but the full-session response-rate contrast was marginal and the significant early-trial analysis was selective.

evidence.design: Within-participant probabilistic monetary instrumental-choice task with counterbalanced fractal assignments.

effect.metric: t statistic for preference toward lower-loss-probability action
effect.notes: t(15)=1.9, one-tailed p<0.05; no confidence interval reported.

evidence.extraction_locator: Materials and Methods, Participants and Stimuli and task; Results, Behavioral Results.
limitations: Small sample and one-tailed significance test.
Neural activation does not identify a causal reinforcer.
evidence.population: Sixteen healthy right-handed adults without reported neurological or psychiatric history.
evidence.summary: Participants preferentially selected the action assigned a lower probability of monetary loss.

evidence.design: Randomized active-avoidance versus yoked-extinction experiment with matched shock and motor exposure and next-day cue-only retrieval.

effect.notes: Active-control participants maintained lower conditioned responding than yoked-extinction participants at next-day retrieval; standardized effect not extracted.

evidence.extraction_locator: Materials and Methods, Subjects and Procedure overview; Results and Abstract.
limitations: This result concerns later physiological threat responding, not direct persistence of avoidance behavior.
Imaging correlates do not establish the mediating neural mechanism.
evidence.population: Fifty-six analyzed healthy adults, 35 female, mean age 23 years; 28 per group.
evidence.summary: Instrumental control over shock omission produced a different next-day threat-response pattern than matched passive extinction.

metadata.description: Seven source-specific extractions from human controlled experiments. Five extractions preserve the separate experiments, including a null result, reported by Fisher and Urcelay (2024); two use independent monetary-loss and yoked shock-control paradigms.
metadata.title: Primary evidence pack for negative reinforcement and active avoidance

objects.definition: Human instrumental test in which an avoidance response to one ambiguous stimulus produces a trained safety signal and a matched response to another stimulus produces no signal or a control signal.
objects.label: Response-produced safety-signal avoidance test
objects.scope: Fisher and Urcelay human experiments using novel Gabor test stimuli.

objects.definition: Human choice task with counterbalanced actions assigned different probabilities of monetary loss.
objects.label: Monetary-loss instrumental avoidance task
objects.scope: Kim, Shimojo, and O'Doherty 2006 instrumental task.

objects.definition: Between-participant task in which an active group can prevent shock by an action and a yoked group receives matched cue, shock, and motor exposure without instrumental control.
objects.label: Active-control versus yoked-extinction task
objects.scope: Boeke et al. 2017 two-day fMRI and psychophysiology experiment.

objects.definition: Observable action whose occurrence changes an aversive consequence or produces a learned safety signal under a specified contingency.
objects.function_note: Avoidance function is assigned only within the stated response-consequence contingency.
objects.label: Instrumental avoidance response
objects.response_topography: Task-specific key press, choice, mouse click, or grid movement.

objects.definition: Programmed aversive image, loud tone, monetary loss, or electric shock.
objects.label: Aversive stimulus outcome

objects.definition: Non-occurrence of the programmed aversive outcome following a successful response.
objects.label: Aversive-outcome omission

boundary_notes: The signal is not identical to subjective relief.
Sensory reinforcement and stimulus generalization require explicit control conditions.
objects.definition: Presentation of the signal previously produced after successful avoidance and tested as a response-contingent consequence.
objects.label: Trained safety-signal presentation

objects.definition: Time-indexed conditioned physiological response to a cue previously paired with shock.
objects.label: Conditioned threat-response state

objects.comparator: Matched ambiguous stimulus followed by no signal or a perceptually controlled new signal.
objects.definition: Dependency in which an instrumental avoidance response produces a trained safety signal during an extinction test, relative to no signal or a new control signal.
objects.label: Response-produced safety-signal contingency
objects.schedule: Eight extinction-test trials per stimulus, except Experiment 5 used eight simultaneous-choice trials.
objects.temporal_relation: Response precedes immediate signal presentation; response frequency is compared across contingencies.

objects.comparator: Alternative action assigned the higher monetary-loss probability.
objects.definition: Counterbalanced dependency assigning one action a lower probability of monetary loss than its alternative.
objects.label: Assigned monetary-loss probability contingency
objects.temporal_relation: Assigned probabilities govern repeated feedback and precede measured preference.

objects.comparator: Yoked cue, shock, and motor exposure without instrumental control.
objects.definition: Dependency allowing a learned grid-movement response to prevent shock, contrasted with yoked participants lacking response-outcome control.
objects.label: Active shock-control contingency
objects.temporal_relation: Active-control training occurs on day 1 before cue-only threat-response testing on day 2.

objects.definition: Proposed learning process in which a response-produced signal associated with aversive-outcome omission increases later instrumental responding.
objects.label: Conditioned safety-signal reinforcement
realization_conditions: The safety signal has a learning history related to successful aversive-outcome omission.
Signal production is contingent on the measured response.
A matched response with no signal or a controlled alternative signal is available for comparison.

objects.definition: Experimental assignment permitting a learned action to prevent an otherwise scheduled shock.
objects.delivery: Grid-movement avoidance task during conditioned threat-cue presentations.
objects.label: Active opportunity to control shock

objects.definition: Count or rate of predefined avoidance actions within eligible test trials.
objects.label: Avoidance-response frequency
objects.method: Compare within-person responses under trained-signal and control contingencies.

objects.definition: Probability or proportion of choices selecting the action with the lower assigned aversive-outcome probability.
objects.label: Avoidance-choice probability
objects.method: Repeated forced choice between counterbalanced fractal actions.

objects.definition: Cue-elicited skin-conductance response used as an index of conditioned physiological threat responding.
objects.label: Skin-conductance threat response
objects.method: Skin conductance recorded during cue presentations and contrasted by cue and experimental group.

sources.title: Safety signals reinforce instrumental avoidance in humans

sources.title: Is Avoiding an Aversive Outcome Rewarding? Neural Substrates of Avoidance Learning in the Human Brain

sources.authority_note: Open randomized human active-control experiment with yoked shock and motor exposure and delayed psychophysiological testing.
sources.title: Active Avoidance: Neural Mechanisms and Attenuation of Pavlovian Conditioned Responding
